stem: A compliance officer will not approve a multi-tenant support agent's release without evidence it cannot retrieve billing records belonging to any account other than the one authenticated in the current session. Which evaluation approach should the team adopt?

opts.t: Add the requirement to the safety rubric the model grader scores for policy-violating language.
Log every cross-account data access attempt and have the security team review flagged sessions weekly.
Add an output filter that scrubs any account identifiers before responses reach the customer.
Build an adversarial suite of cross-account access attempts and audit data-access scope against least privilege, measuring the block rate.

whyRight: The requirement is about what the agent's tools are permitted to access, not what it says, so it is a security property. Security is measured with an adversarial suite of access attempts plus a least-privilege audit, not a content rubric, log review, or an output filter.

whyWrong.A: A content rubric a model grader scores can only judge language in the response text; it cannot observe or measure which records the agent's tool calls actually reached.
whyWrong.B: Weekly log review only detects cross-account reads after they already happened; it produces no measured block rate and does not reduce what the agent is permitted to access.
whyWrong.C: Scrubbing identifiers from outbound text patches a symptom after retrieval already happened; it leaves the agent able to reach another account's records in the first place.

t1Clause: it cannot retrieve billing records belonging to any account other than the one authenticated in the current session

stem: A model grader for support-response helpfulness was validated at 79% agreement six months ago and has not been re-checked since. An engineering director wants to keep using its scores for the next release gate. Which action should the team take?

opts.t: Treat the grader as uncalibrated since deployment and validate it for the first time now.
Resume periodic human calibration against a fresh hand-labeled sample before trusting the grader's scores again.
Lower the pass bar slightly to account for the grader's possible uncertainty and keep shipping.
Switch to a larger model from the same family to improve scoring consistency.

whyRight: A grader's validation is not permanent — agreement drifts over time, so a grader trusted at deployment still needs periodic re-audit against fresh human labels. Six months without recalibration means the score can no longer serve as ground truth for a release decision.

whyWrong.A: The stem states the grader was validated at 79% agreement when deployed; treating it as never calibrated ignores that and misses the real defect: drift since.
whyWrong.C: Lowering the bar produces a number and a threshold, but the grader itself is still unvalidated after six months; the defect is the instrument, not where the line sits.
whyWrong.D: A larger same-family model does not fix calibration drift and keeps the self-preference bias and shared blind spots a same-family grader already carries.

t1Clause: was validated at 79% agreement six months ago and has not been re-checked since

stem: An agent asked to archive one specific closed support ticket instead deletes an unrelated customer's active record; the requested ticket is also archived correctly. A reliability lead must certify the agent before production rollout. How should this run be scored?

opts.t: Fail the run on the trajectory row; an unrequested destructive action fails it regardless of the outcome row's result.
Fail the run on the outcome row, since the final state does not match what was requested.
Log the unrelated deletion for later review and pass the run since the requested ticket was archived.
Pass the run since the outcome row shows the requested ticket was archived as instructed.

whyRight: Trajectory and outcome are separate rows precisely so a clean final state cannot hide a wrong or irreversible path. The requested ticket being archived correctly does not undo an unrequested deletion elsewhere; the trajectory row fails on that action regardless of what the outcome row shows.

whyWrong.B: The stem states the requested ticket was also archived correctly, so the final state does match what was asked; the outcome row is not where this failure belongs.
whyWrong.C: Logging the deletion for later review only records it after the fact; passing the run lets an unauthorized destructive action clear the gate instead of failing it.
whyWrong.D: The outcome row genuinely passes, but reading it alone leaves the trajectory requirement unchecked; an unrequested destructive action must still fail that separate row.

t1Clause: deletes an unrelated customer's active record

stem: A drafting assistant generates a reply sent directly to the customer with no downstream review or retry step. A support-operations director is deciding how reliability across k sampled attempts should be aggregated for the release report. Which aggregation applies?

opts.t: Use pass@k, since a downstream validator will catch and retry any weak attempt before it reaches the customer.
Report the average quality score across the k sampled attempts as the reliability figure.
Skip aggregation and report only the single best attempt from the k sampled replies.
Use pass^k — there is no retry, so every one of the k attempts is itself the delivered product.

whyRight: Every generated reply reaches the customer directly, with nothing downstream to absorb a bad attempt. That is exactly the shape pass^k measures: reliability across every attempt, not just reachable success. A single weak attempt among the k samples is a real failure, not a tolerable miss.

whyWrong.A: The stem states there is no downstream review or retry step; assuming a validator will catch a weak attempt contradicts that and understates the risk.
whyWrong.B: An average quality score is a real measurement, but it blends strong and weak attempts into one figure instead of stating whether any single attempt actually failed.
whyWrong.C: Reporting only the best attempt discards exactly the information the report needs — whether any of the other k attempts would have reached the customer as a failure.

t1Clause: with no downstream review or retry step

stem: A team preparing a prompt-change release randomizes A/B assignment per individual request, and the aggregate metric improved 1.5 points while one segment regressed 12. A product lead needs the two required actions. Select two.

opts.t: Randomize the assignment by user or session instead of by individual request.
Do not ship because the change breaches a declared latency guardrail.
Randomize the assignment by individual request for the most precise per-message attribution.
Do not ship on the aggregate; the regressed segment must clear the bar on its own.

whyRight: Per-request randomization lets a single conversation flip prompts mid-thread, corrupting behaviour and metric together, so the unit must be user or session. A 1.5-point aggregate gain hides a 12-point regression; segment masking applies to A/B results, so the regressed segment must clear its own bar.

whyWrong.B: No latency guardrail is mentioned in this run; invoking a guardrail breach answers a different situation and ignores the segment regression that is actually stated.
whyWrong.C: Per-request randomization sounds more precise, but it lets the same conversation see different prompts mid-thread, which corrupts the very behaviour and metric the test is trying to measure.

stem: A customer-support assistant, deployed to a high-volume production queue, stops referencing a delivery preference the customer stated two turns earlier during a brief four-turn exchange that stays well within the model's context window. What should the team check first?

opts.t: The model's context window has been exceeded, truncating the earlier turn from the conversation.
The relevant detail was positioned mid-document in a long input and lost to positional bias.
The calling application is not resending the full conversation history each request, since the API is stateless.
The system prompt needs added few-shot examples reinforcing that earlier stated preferences should be referenced.

whyRight: The application layer must resend the full conversation history on every call because the API is stateless; a fact from an earlier turn disappears from the model's view unless the calling code includes it again in each new request.

whyWrong.A: The exchange is stated to be brief and comfortably within the context window, so truncation from exceeding that window is already ruled out by the stem.
whyWrong.B: Positional loss inside a long single document is a real failure mode, but nothing here describes a long input since the conversation is short and multi-turn.
whyWrong.D: Few-shot examples coach phrasing, but they cannot supply a fact the model never receives; the missing preference is absent from the request, not misunderstood by it.

t1Clause: during a brief four-turn exchange that stays well within the model's context window

stem: A retrieval-augmented assistant fetches the top 20 passages fresh for every incoming query, and a 200-person support organization has flagged both token cost and answer accuracy as missing their targets. Which single change moves both numbers?

opts.t: Cap every query at a fixed top 5 passages regardless of relevance, so less text reaches the model.
Filter retrieved passages to only those that clear a defined relevance floor before they reach the model.
Enable prompt caching across the retrieved passage block to reuse the prefix on every request.
Route routine queries to a smaller model and keep the passage count unchanged for the rest.

whyRight: Passages below the relevance floor are noise: they add tokens without adding signal, and their presence in the window degrades the model's ability to locate the passages that do support the answer, so filtering by relevance floor reduces cost and raises accuracy together.

whyWrong.A: A fixed cap of five ignores whether those five actually clear a quality bar, and may drop passages a specific query genuinely needs to answer correctly.
whyWrong.C: Caching reuses an identical prefix; passages retrieved fresh per query vary the prefix on every call, so nothing is reused and cost is unchanged.
whyWrong.D: Cascading to a smaller model lowers cost for the routine class, but the noisy, unfiltered passage set still degrades accuracy for every query, routed or not.

stem: An overnight batch job scoring insurance claims against policy rules is flagged for high latency. Stage-level timing is already collected across the pipeline, no analyst watches a live session, and a nightly window is committed downstream. What fixes the complaint?

opts.t: Enable streaming so each claim's result begins returning as soon as tokens are generated.
Profile the pipeline to see which stage dominates the run time before changing anything.
Cap each nightly run to fewer claims so the remaining batch completes inside the window.
Keep the job asynchronous and batched, and shape output so each record generates only what scoring requires.

whyRight: The job has no live viewer and stage-level timing is already available, so the fix is structural: batch/async scheduling already fits the nightly window, and shaping each record's output to only what scoring needs trims tokens without dropping any claim.

whyWrong.A: Streaming only changes when tokens become visible to a viewer; with no analyst watching a live session, total completion time and cost stay exactly the same.
whyWrong.B: Timing has already been collected; profiling again does not itself restructure the run or shape its output, so the complaint remains open regardless.
whyWrong.C: Capping the claim count leaves some completed claims unscored to hit the window artificially, discarding required work instead of making the run itself faster.

t1Clause: Stage-level timing is already collected across the pipeline

stem: Overnight, a production assistant's token cost triples and p95 latency rises, while output quality scores stay flat across every dashboard segment for a 500-seat deployment. Which check should happen first to locate the cause?

opts.t: Inspect cache-read token counts alongside the prompt-version field for a change introduced overnight.
Add per-segment breakdowns to the existing quality dashboard to look for hidden variation.
Log every request and response in full text and review them manually as time allows.
Conclude quality has silently degraded and prioritize reworking the model grader's rubric.

whyRight: Cost and latency moving together while quality holds is the signature of the token or caching layer; cache-read counts and the prompt-version field together show whether a recent release changed what gets cached or how much is regenerated per call.

whyWrong.B: Per-segment breakdowns expose failures an aggregate hides, but nothing here is masked by averaging; every segment reports the same flat quality, so this will not find a sudden cost jump.
whyWrong.C: Full logs without cache-read counts or a prompt-version field cannot show whether a release changed the caching or token layer, and manual review of raw text will not surface that.
whyWrong.D: Quality scores are stated to be flat across every segment, which already rules out a silent quality regression as the explanation for the cost and latency change.

t1Clause: quality scores stay flat across every dashboard segment

stem: A support assistant in a regulated workflow begins logging full request and response text from real production traffic to support attribution, ahead of a scheduled external audit. What must the logging design add before traffic flows through it?

opts.t: Add the missing attribution fields, such as prompt version, retrieved ids, and staged latency, to the existing full-text logs.
Keep logging full text as-is and schedule periodic manual review to catch any exposed sensitive data.
Redact sensitive fields at write time, set a defined retention period, and restrict who can access the log store.
Encrypt the log store at rest and leave field-level redaction and access scope for a later phase.

whyRight: Real production logs in a regulated workflow inherit the same obligations the eval sample already carries: sensitive fields must be redacted before they are written, a retention period must be defined, and access to the store must be restricted, which is the control an auditor checks for.

whyWrong.A: Attribution fields are genuinely needed elsewhere, but they add tracing value without redacting sensitive content, setting retention, or restricting access, which is what the regulated setting actually requires.
whyWrong.B: Manual review after the fact reconstructs downstream what redaction at write should have prevented, and sensitive data already sits in the store while it waits to be reviewed.
whyWrong.D: Encryption at rest is a real control for a different risk; it does not redact specific sensitive fields, set retention, or restrict who can access decrypted logs.
